title: Relative Ranks
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing every athlete against every other one versus sorting indices by score once and deriving rank directly from position.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array score representing the scores of athletes in a competition (all scores distinct), the athletes with the top 3 scores receive "Gold Medal," "Silver Medal," and "Bronze Medal," and the rest receive their placement number as a string ("4", "5", and so on). Return an array of these rank strings, in the original order of score.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Determine each athlete's placement based on their score (highest score is 1st place), assign medal names to the top 3, and plain placement numbers to the rest, all while preserving the original input order in the output.

blocks.title: Analogy: Announcing Race Results in Bib-Number Order
blocks.text: Picture a race where runners finish in some order, but results must be announced in bib-number order (their original lineup), not finish order. Sorting the finish times once, then looking up each runner's placement, is far faster than comparing every runner's time against every other runner's individually.

blocks.caption: Sort once; position in that sorted order directly gives the rank

blocks.text: Since the scores are already in descending order, the result is ["Gold Medal", "Silver Medal", "Bronze Medal", "4", "5"].
Sorted descending, the scores are 10, 9, 8, 4, 3; mapping back to original positions gives ["Gold Medal", "5", "Bronze Medal", "Silver Medal", "4"].
Before comparing every athlete's score against every other athlete's individually, notice that sorting once immediately reveals every athlete's placement.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An athlete's rank is exactly 1 plus the number of athletes with a strictly higher score.

Observation 2: Sorting all scores in descending order directly produces this rank as the position in that sorted list.

Observation 3: To preserve the original input order in the output, sort the INDICES by their scores, not the scores themselves, so each index can be mapped back to its original position afterward.

Observation 4: Assigning "Gold Medal," "Silver Medal," "Bronze Medal" to the first 3 positions in this sorted order, and the placement number to the rest, completes the mapping.
This leads to sorting the athlete indices by score once, then directly assigning rank strings based on position in that sorted order, written back into the original index positions.
For each athlete, count how many other athletes have a strictly higher score, giving that athlete's rank directly.

items: For every athlete, compare their score against every other athlete's score.
Count how many scores are strictly higher; that count plus 1 is the rank.
Convert the rank to a medal name (for 1st, 2nd, 3rd) or its plain number.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: for each athlete, count how many others scored higher

codes.python:
def find_relative_ranks(score):
    n = len(score)
    result = [None] * n
    medals = ['Gold Medal', 'Silver Medal', 'Bronze Medal']
    for i in range(n):
        rank = 1
        for j in range(n):
            if score[j] > score[i]:                # compare against every other athlete
                rank += 1
        result[i] = medals[rank - 1] if rank <= 3 else str(rank)
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every athlete's rank is computed independently, by comparing against every other athlete directly.
This repeats essentially the same comparisons many times over, once per athlete pair.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), comparing every pair of athletes.
Space: O(n) for the result.
Limitation: a single sort reveals every athlete's relative rank at once, making the pairwise comparison approach far more work than necessary.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why pairwise comparison is wasteful: sorting the scores once directly produces every athlete's rank as their position in that sorted order, no repeated comparisons needed.

How to preserve the original order in the output: sort the INDICES of the array by score, not the scores themselves, so each sorted position can be traced back to where it came from originally.

The core idea: sort indices by score descending once; the position in that order is the rank, assigned back to the original index.

Create a list of indices 0 through n minus 1, and sort it by score in descending order. Walk through this sorted list of indices; the position (0-indexed) in this walk plus 1 is that athlete's rank. Assign "Gold Medal," "Silver Medal," "Bronze Medal" for ranks 1 through 3, and the plain rank number as a string otherwise, writing each result back to its original index.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: sort indices by score once, position directly gives the rank

codes.python:
def find_relative_ranks(score):
    n = len(score)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -score[i])   # sort indices by score, descending, once
    result = [None] * n
    medals = ['Gold Medal', 'Silver Medal', 'Bronze Medal']
    for rank, i in enumerate(order):
        result[i] = medals[rank] if rank < 3 else str(rank + 1)
    return result

blocks.text: Sorting the indices by score in descending order directly places the highest-scoring athlete's index first, the second-highest second, and so on, exactly matching each athlete's true rank as a position in this single sorted pass. Writing each result back to its ORIGINAL index (rather than the sorted position) correctly restores the input order in the final output.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(n) for the index array and result.

blocks.text: Relative Ranks is a straightforward "sort once, derive everything from position" problem; the only subtlety is sorting INDICES rather than values, so the original input order can be restored in the final output.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the output must stay in original order", think: sort the indices by score, not the values themselves.

items: How would this change if scores could tie, and ties needed to share the same rank?
How would you support this efficiently if athletes' scores were updated frequently, needing re-ranking each time?
Any "assign rank based on sorted position, but preserve original order" problem, solved by sorting indices instead of values.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized single-sort approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: sort indices by value once, deriving rank directly from sorted position.
Core Idea: sort the athlete indices by score descending; the position in that sorted order is the rank, written back to the original index for the final output.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: sorting indices (not values) is what allows the original input order to be restored in the output.
Interview Difficulty: a straightforward sorting problem, quick once the index-sorting trick is applied.
One line memory trick: sort indices by score; position is the rank.
